content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this work, the authors propose an approach for improving Markov Chain Monte Carlo inference of the posterior over the weights of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) with Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) architectures. They argue that a major challenge in MCMC inference in BNNs is that, due to the weight-space symmetries of BNNs, different Markov Chains may yield samples which correspond to the same function in the output space, failing to capture a diverse set of functions which are supported by the posterior.

In particular, the authors propose an algorithm for addressing two kinds of symmetries in the posterior:
1. Permutation symmetries due to swapping the input and output weights of two neurons in the same layer.
2. Sign symmetries in MLPs with anti-symmetric activations, i.e. activations which satisfy $a(-x) = -a(x)$.

The authors introduce two corresponding procedures which, after performing several parallel MCMC runs, transform the samples in such a way that weights which give rise to the same function in the output-space are mapped to the same weight in the weight-space. They propose running several independently initialised Markov Chains to encourage exploration of all functionally diverse modes of the posterior. They derive a lower bound on the probability that the number $G$ of independently initialised Markov Chains necessary to visit all functionally diverse modes of the posterior is larger than a pre-specified budget $\rho$. They use this $\rho$ to decide on the number of Markov Chains to run at inference time.

The authors claim that their symmetry removal procedure, together with their criterion for picking $\rho$ improves the performance of the model, and evaluate the performance of their approach against the Laplace approximation (LA) and Deep Ensembles (DE) on standard handcrafted datasets and UCI datasets. They also claim their procedure improves the interpretability of the samples, since after the symmetry removal procedure, the different modes of the samples correspond to different functions in the output space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

**An interesting symmetry removal algorithm:** The authors introduce an interesting symmetry removal approach. While the paper has several important weaknesses, the proposed algorithm does in fact eliminate the symmetries that the authors investigate from a set of samples drawn via MCMC.

**Interpretability:** The authors' method appears interesting from the standpoint of interpreting the posteriors of BNNs. In particular, it presents some promise for investigating the posteriors of BNNs by eliminating certain symmetries in the weight space, and making the resulting samples more interpretable by human investigators. Their method also makes downstream clustering of the weights much easier, since it drastically reduces the number of modes, so that clustering approaches with far fewer clusters may be run.

## Weaknesses

**Unclear if the proposed method can improve performance:** It is unclear whether the proposed method can improve the predictive performance of the resulting models, or better handle functionally diverse modes, compared to just performing MCMC without symmetry removal. My reasoning for this is as follows. The authors assume we are given an MLP architecture $M$ parameterised by weights $\theta \in \Theta$, and activation $a$. Given $M$, there exists a class of equioutput transformations $\mathcal{E}$ such that

$$ p(y | x, \theta, M) = p(y | x, E(\theta), M) \text{ for all } x \in \mathcal{X}, \theta \in \Theta, E \in \mathcal{E}. $$

Given a prior $p(\theta)$ and observed data $D$, they assume access to an MCMC procedure $\texttt{MCMC}$ which yields a (possibly approximate) sample $\theta$ from the posterior $p(\theta | D)$ of the network weights, that is

$$\theta \sim \texttt{MCMC}(\theta; A, D) \approx p(\theta | D).$$

They then introduce a symmetry removal algorithm $\texttt{SR}$ which maps all weight settings which are equal up to an equioutput transformation, to a single representative weight setting which corresponds to the same output function as the original weights. Specifically, this means that for any $\theta', \theta'' \in \Theta$, if there exists $E \in \mathcal{E}$ such that $\theta' = E(\theta'')$, then

$$\texttt{SR}(\theta') = \texttt{SR}(\theta'') \text{ and } p(y | x, \theta', M) = p(y | x, \texttt{SR}(\theta'), M). $$

Now, from the above, if we draw $N$ (possibly approximate) samples $\theta_n \sim \texttt{MCMC}(\theta; A, D)$, it holds that

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N p(y^* | x^*, \theta_n, M) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N p(y^* | x^*, \texttt{SR}(\theta_n), M). $$

Therefore, the predictions of a model where we first apply $\texttt{MCMC}$ and then $\texttt{SR}$ are *identical* to the predictions of the model where we simply perform $\texttt{MCMC}$ without any symmetry removal. It appears that *applying symmetry removal after running MCMC* does not change the predictions of the model and therefore *cannot improve its performance*. Furthermore, this procedure does not make the MCMC procedure any more efficient, since the authors propose running a standard chain, and then transforming the sampled weights in a way which leaves model predictions invariant. **I would welcome any clarifications on this from the authors, in case I have misunderstood their argument.**

**Lack of rigor in the assumptions of Proposition 2:** In Proposition 2, the authors state a lower bound on the probability that the number $G$ of independently initialised Markov Chains necessary to visit all functionally diverse modes of the posterior is larger than a pre-specified budget $\rho$. Specifically, they say 

> Let $\pi_1, ..., \pi_\nu$ be the respective probabilities of $\nu$ independently started Markov chains to land in the corresponding functionally diverse mode.

This statement has a couple of issues. The first is that the authors probably intended to say something like

> Let $\pi_1, ..., \pi_\nu$ be the respective probabilities of a Markov chain to land in the corresponding functionally diverse mode, and suppose $\rho$ Markov chains are initialised independently and with an identical initial distribution.

since the number of the Markov chains initialised is $\rho$ and not $\nu$. **Is this a typographical error?** The second issue is that the authors never explain what "landing in the corresponding mode means". For example, does it mean for a sample to fall at a point from which following gradient descent (with an infinitesimal step size) converges to a mode? **Clarification on this would be much appreciated, and very beneficial to the argumentation of the paper.**

**Lack of comments on the probability of visiting all modes:** The authors make no comments on the feasibility of visiting all modes. For example, if most modes are easy to get to for the Markov chain (i.e. the Markov chain has high probability of getting to these modes), except for one mode which is very hard to get to (i.e. the Markov chain has very low probability of getting to this mode), then the number of chains required can presumably be very large. This is likely a crucial issue if one wants to visit all functional modes with MCMC, and could adversely affect results if the hard-to-get-to mode has large mass. The authors make no comment on this issue. **Further clarification in the review phase and in the paper would be appreciated.**

**Number of functionally diverse modes:** The authors claim that

> In our experiments in Section 6, we find $\nu$ to be rather small $\nu < 10$.

First, the number of modes is not known a-priori. Therefore, we won't know $\nu$ in advance and simply be able to run the appropriate number of $\rho$ chains in parallel. In order to save computation, it seems that some small number $\rho'$ of chains must be run in advance so that $\nu$ can be inferred, following a larger run of $\rho$ chains, for example. **The submission would benefit from clarification on this issue.**

Second, and related to the above, if for some problem the number of functionally diverse modes is in fact large, then the number of the chains $G$ needed to visit them all will also be very large, and running a correspondingly large number of chains $\rho$ becomes infeasible. **Again, clarification on this would be much appreciated, and beneficial to the argumentation of the paper.**

**Unusually large error bars in Table 1:** In Section 6.1, Table 1, the authors report the predictive performance of the Laplace approximation (LA) and Deep Ensembles (DE), which do not seem credible. In particular, some of the results of LA and DE have extremely large error bars when applied to standard benchmarks, which suggests that the methods may have been applied in an improper manner. For example, for the Concrete dataset, using the architecture $f_1$, the authors report an LLPD of $-14.49 \pm 14.69$ using LA, and $-4.36 \pm 6.48$ using Deep Ensembles (DE). The authors also do not include sufficient details in Appendix F in order for their results to be reproduced, making it hard to check why LA and DE performed poorly in their experiments. **Further clarification in the rebuttal phase and in the paper would be appreciated.**

**Faulty reporting of statistically significant results:** In Section 6.1, Table 1, the authors have boldfaced the column corresponding to their results, claiming it is "the best method" when compared to LA and DE. However, the error bars of the reported methods are often overlapping, which means that one cannot confidently decide whether their method is in fact the best one, in a statistically significant way. Furthermore, the authors do not explain what the error bars are showing: Is this one (or two) standard deviations aggregated over predictions for individual datapoints? Does it involve multiple repetitions of the same experiment with different random seeds? **Further clarification in the rebuttal phase and in the paper would be appreciated. I would recommend using boldface only if a method is better in a statistically significant way.**
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The paper is reasonably written, but its clarity could be improved. For example, the authors claim that:

> Removing [such] functional redundancies enables exact uncertainty quantification in a reduced posterior space and thus improves over local approximations.

However, it is unclear whether this method helps with predictive performance at all (see argument in the Strengths and Weaknesses section above). Furthermore, inference is performed by MCMC in the original weight space, so the term "exact uncertainty quantification in a reduced posterior space" is somewhat misleading. I recommend that the authors should clarify this point (throughout the paper) as it confuses the messaging of this work.

Further, the authors often use confusing phrases, which are not properly explained, such as:

> [In appendix] ... while often yielding satisfactory results in practice, crudely disregard the posterior geometry.

> [In section 3, functional redundancy] ... do not respect the geometry of the posterior distribution and removable symmetries between modes remain.

Regarding the above, what do the authors mean when they say "posterior geometry", and why is disregarding it a problem?

> [In section 4] ... the neural network parameter space $\Theta$ can [...] be dissected into $|\mathcal{E}|$ disjunctive sets of the same cardinality.

Regarding the above, isn't the cardinality of each of these sets infinitely uncountable? How is the cardinality of the sets relevant to the discussion presented here?

> [Proposition 2] Let $\pi_1, ..., \pi_\nu$ be the respective probabilities of $\nu$ independently started Markov chains to land in the corresponding functionally diverse mode.

What does it mean to "land in a mode" and what is "a functionally diverse mode"? See also discussion above, in the Strengths and Weaknesses section.

**Quality:** Overall the quality of the paper is somewhat lacking, both in terms of theoretical rigour and clarity, as well as in terms of the experimental results. I highly encourage the authors to address some of the related issues described in the Strengths and Weaknesses section. The most important of these issues is that is seems like the symmetry removal method presented by the authors could not possibly affect the predictive power of the models, yet it is presented as such.

**Novelty:** The moral of this paper (removing posterior symmetries which arise from invariances in permutations of the neurons and flipping of the signs of the weights) is not entirely new and, as the authors point out, has been explored in previous work. However, the specific approach for removing symmetries appears novel and may be of further interest in terms of interpretability. 

**Reproducibility:** While the authors give some information on their experimental setup in Appendix F, more details are required in order to reproduce their experimental results. Some of these include:

- Additional details on the MCMC procedure: the authors do not provide details on their MCMC procedure, including for example any hyperparameters used.
- The details of the Laplace approximation method. Did the authors sample from the Laplace approximate posterior or did they use a generalised linear model approximation as in Immer et al. 2021?
- Additional details on the Deep Ensembles: the authors mention in Appendix F that they trained their DE using full-batch training. How did they initialise the weights and was there any data bootstrapping used as in Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017?

As a general rule, it is a good principle to provide enough details about the experimental setup such that a reviewer or interested reader is able to reproduce the results of the paper exactly, up to random seeding, or other minor details.


**References**

A Immer, M Korzepa, M Bauer, Improving predictions of Bayesian neural nets via local linearization, 2021.

B Lakshminarayanan, A Pritzel, C Blundell, Simple and scalable predictive uncertainty estimation using deep ensembles, 2017.
content.summary_of_the_review:
**Summary:** In summary, I think the authors' idea is an interesting one, but the work at its current shape has several issues. The most central of these issues is that, it seems like removing the symmetries present in a set of MCMC samples post hoc, does not improve improve predictive performance, neither does it make MCMC itself more efficient. The paper also appears to have some issues in terms of clarity and rigour. I welcome the authors' rebuttal, in case I have misunderstood their arguments, or if they have further clarification to provide. 

That said, I think that one of the more interesting parts of the paper is that removing symmetries can potentially make the clustering of different modes of the samples much easier, which could lead to promising research directions. Perhaps the authors should consider focusing more in this aspect of the paper.

**Recommendation:** I therefore recommend the paper for a score of 3, with a confidence score of 3, because while the paper has several important issues it may be the case I have misunderstood the authors' argument. Further, I am very happy to adjust my overall score (and partial scores) if the authors are able to clarify and support their statements made in the paper, and respond to the issues pointed out above.

content.title: Individual response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful remarks on our proposal and would like to comment on the points not addressed in the general answer.

### Report of results in Table 1 and missing information
In Table 1 we provided one standard deviation over posterior samples and we will clarify this in the revised version of the manuscript. Furthermore we will provide missing information on the experimental setup and adapt our description of the MCMC part in the introduction of Section 6.

### Unclear text passages 
As pointed out by the reviewer, we have now rephrased statements about the posterior geometry and functionally diverse modes in the new version of the manuscript. By posterior geometry we follow the wording of Frühwirth-Schnatter (2001), characterizing the probability landscape of the posterior distribution in a topological sense, where we view the posterior distribution as a hypersurface in the weight space. By “disregarding the geometry in approximation methods” we mean the phenomenon of omitting functionally relevant parts of the posterior, as strictly local approximations like LA do (shown in Section 6.4). On the other hand, “disrespecting the geometry” of the posterior in the symmetry removal process refers to the possibility of an identifiability constraint intersecting a mode, which would result in an incomplete removal of its symmetric copies.

### Lack of comments on the probability of visiting all modes
A low mode probability results in an higher amount of estimated MCMC chains, which is why we intended to choose a fair example with at least one mode of relatively low probability. However, having multiple such modes or even lower mode probabilities in fact increases the number of chains quickly. But the practitioner can choose to estimate the number of chains with respect to a probability cut-off, excluding highly unlikely modes in their experiments which do not have a major contribution to the posterior.

### Lack of rigor in the assumptions of Proposition 2
By “landing in a mode” with an MCMC chain we indeed mean, as the reviewer suggested, that gradient descent following from a sample converges to a posterior mode.
We further thank the reviewer for pointing out the typographical error in Proposition 2. We indeed meant $\rho$ and not $\nu$ in the beginning of the Proposition.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength 

- The problem to solve is important and the paper is well-motivated. 

# Weaknesses
- The writing and organization of this paper should be significantly improved. I have trouble understanding some key concepts in this paper. First, is Proposition 2 a novel result developed by you or from relevant literature? You should make it clear. Besides, by saying "posterior symmetry removal", what is the meaning? What is the difference between it and regular symmetry removal algorithms in deep learning? Moreover, it is hard to determine your technical novelty based on the current expression. To how much extent does the proposed method rely on the approach from Fruhwirth-Schnatter (2001)?
- The method is restrictive to MLPs with tanh activations. This largely undermines the applicability and implication of this paper. If we can only use MLPs to achieve exact inference, why not just leverage the connections between (infinite-width) MLPs and NN-GPs to achieve analytical inference? What's more, NN-GP is shown to be a strong baseline for regression tasks. Can you provide a direct comparison between your method and NN-GPs?
- Will the choice of MCMC sampler significantly affect the outcomes under the proposed symmetry removal?
- What's the time/storage cost of MCMC under symmetry removal? Is it cheaper than DE and LA when performing similarly?

content.title: Individual response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful remarks on our proposal and would like to comment on the points not addressed in the general answer.

### Comparison to NN-GPs
NN-GPs enjoy many favorable properties and often provide good solutions, so a direct comparison may indeed be interesting. Note, however, that our proposal should, in fact, provide a fair comparison and ideally compare to algorithms that are as close to the ground truth as possible. Our proposal should be architecture-agnostic and all competitor methods should be based on the same architecture as we want to encourage the use of MCMC rather than approximate inference methods, not improve predictive performance. 

### MCMC sampler choice and effect
Since the symmetry removal algorithm acts post-hoc on the samples obtained from MCMC, the outcome will not be affected by the choice of the sampler, provided the samples approximate the posterior sufficiently well. We found that the use of the No-U Turn Sampler (NUTS) for BNNs worked best in our case.

### Relation to previous work
The algorithm only follows the principle of Frühwirth-Schnatter by working in a selected parameter subspace of equioutput transformation related parameters, which is helpful for finding identifiability constraints. However the approach of finding these constraints is completely unrelated. We now make this more clear in the revised version of our paper.

### Time complexity
We do not intend to provide a computationally less expensive method compared to deep ensembles or the Laplace approximation. Motivated by the superior predictive performance of MCMC, instead we aim to make MCMC computational feasible for arbitrary BNNs by focusing on the symmetry-free posterior distribution and providing the computable upper bound for the number of MCMC chains for a proper exploration.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. This is a very important problem and very relevant to ICLR. 

2. The paper is well-written and mostly easy to follow. 

3. I liked the plots and small-scale visualisations in the Figures, they helped build intuition and confirm the method is doing what the authors claim. 

4. I like the method and its application to neural networks. It is a neat idea and is well-applied in the paper. 

**Weaknesses**

5. I strongly recommend having a paragraph/few lines in the introduction highlighting that this paper only tests on very small scale neural networks, and the experiments are proof-of-concept. (Perhaps even add a phrase like this in the Abstract?) Note that I do not have an issue with the fact that the experiments are small-scale, this is fine for a paper, as the method is neat and there is enough novelty in the paper already in my opinion. 

6. I would like to see some kind of computation cost analysis. That can be as a theoretical computation cost of the algorithm, or as reporting runtime of the algorithm compared to other algorithms in the results. (Again, it is OK if this is significantly worse than other algorithms, as I expect, but this should still be reported.) 

7. Is setting $nu$ to 3 a big assumption? How would this scale with larger neural networks? Presumably this parameter would rise, and this would be a big reason that the computation cost increases with larger neural networks? I was missing a little intuition here.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the approach to remove model non-identifiability of posterior samples in Bayesian sampling.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weakness: The purpose of symmetry removal is unclear.  Say, MCMC generates g samples, corresponding to g trained models. After removing symmetry, it remains g (different) samples corresponding to exactly the same g trained models. Therefore, the Bayesian inference for the unknown regression function f has no difference, with or without symmetry removal. In other words, all the good performance, e.g., good prediction of Table 1, capable of capturing three modes in figure 4, are purely due to the MCMC sampling, but has nothing to do with the symmetry removal.

The only improvement is that it is easier to reveal the modality structure of the weight posterior distribution after symmetry removal. But I don't see how such information directly helps uncertainty quantifications on f. For instance, what does figure 4 (b)-(d) tell us beyond figure 4 (e), in terms of Bayesian inference?

I have no idea how Proposition 2 helps in practice since the number of modes and mode probabilities are unknown.  

Other contributions seem weak and straightforward.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: page 7: "As in Section 6.1, we assume ν = 3 and mode probabilities as in the given example." Where is this given example?

Novelty: I fail to see any significant insight into the Bayesian uncertainty quantification of DNN from this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to remove the symmetries in the neural network weights for better posterior approximation. Specifically, the authors first show that the distribution of functions can be captured exactly via a small fraction of the distribution of weights. They further provide an upper bound for the number of required Monte Carlo chains in order to cover all diverse modes in the function space. Finally, the authors develop a new algorithm to remove the redundancy in the obtained MCMC samples. The authors have conducted experiments on synthetic datasets to verify the theoretical findings and the proposed symmetry removal algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- The studied problem of removing symmetries in neural network posteriors is important. 

- As far as I understand, using the view of equioutput parametrizations to analyze neural network posteriors is new. The theoretical analysis and the proposed algorithm appear to be technically sound. 

- The authors provide several empirical results to verify the theory. 

- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

 Weaknesses

- The motivation for reducing the obtained samples to the reference set is unclear. If we care about the function distribution, it will be equivalent to using either the reduced weight posterior distribution or the original one. What are the benefits of doing the reduction? In the beginning, I thought the authors first remove the symmetries and then use MCMC to sample from this simplified posterior which will improve sampling efficiency. However, in the paper, the MCMC algorithm still samples from the original highly multimodal distribution. I do not see how it achieves efficient posterior sampling.

- The significance of the theorems is unclear. Proposition 1 directly follows Chen et al. (1993). The practical meaning of Proposition 2 seems unclear and it may be too loose to have practical usage.  In the given example, even if there are only three modes, the bound requires 1274 chains which seems quite large. It may be because the bound is dimensional independent.

- The experiments do not well support the theorems. In Section 6.1, the MCMC method uses 1274 chains whereas the baselines only use 10 models. This seems an unfair comparison. I think it will be better to use the same number of chains/models for all methods for a fair comparison. Besides, I do not see how these results can justify the derived upper bound. It is possible that the MCMC can have similar results with fewer chains.

I do not see why Section 6.2 verifies Corollary 1. It only shows the predictive distribution improves as MCMC collects more samples. 
Section 6.2 empirically shows that the proposed algorithm can remove redundancy in the posterior. But I do not understand why it helps, since the function distribution will be equivalent before and after removal. It might be useful to compare the performance of the posterior before and after removal.

- The proposed symmetry removal algorithm only works for very small neural networks (e.g. a single layer with 16 neurons) and could not be used in practice.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
- In the abstract and introduction, it seems misleading to claim an estimation for the number of MC samples whereas it is the number of MC chains. Because running 1000 chains is far more costly than obtaining 1000 samples.

- I do not find which part of the paper talks about the claimed third contribution “we relate our findings to the state-of-the-art DE and LA methods and provide an explanation for their high-quality uncertainty but also point out their limitations.”

Quality and Novelty: see "Strength And Weaknesses"

Reproducibility: It is unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I think the analysis perspective of this paper is interesting and new. However, the practical meaning of the theory is unclear and the empirical results do not support the theory well.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful remarks on our proposal and would like to comment on the points not addressed in the general answer.

### Unfair comparison
At first glance, restricting the finite-ensemble methods to ten ensemble members while MCMC is allowed 1274 chains might seem to unduly favor MCMC. Please note, however, that our goal here was merely to demonstrate that MCMC can still compete against state-of-the-art approximate Bayesian methods when the upper bound on chains is obeyed. In this regard, a deep ensemble with ten members is arguably a standard choice.

### Experiment Section 6.2 (Corollary 1 support)

Although $f_2$ exhibits a high dimensional parameter space that might seem to exceed the capabilities of MCMC, we want to show that the posterior predictive distribution converges with a comparably small amount of samples. Figure 2 depicts how the approximation quality of the predictive posterior performance saturates already when moving from 256 to 1274 samples, indicating that, in fact, few samples suffice to obtain a good approximation to the posterior predictive in practice.
Note that the purpose of this example is to provide practical evidence for Corollary 1 – that vast amount of parameterizations is redundant  – and that it is independent from the symmetry removal algorithm.

### Relating findings to deep ensembles and Laplace approximation
Focusing on the symmetry-free BNN posterior as provided in the experimental section reveals unimodal distributions of parameters in Section 6.3 explaining the good performance of LA in certain cases. Section 6.4, on the other hand, reveals a symmetry-free BNN posterior exhibiting three functionally diverse modes, which is a case where LA would not be able to fully capture all uncertainty. This is also where the improvement of DE over LA stems from in our opinion. We added the last statement to the manuscript as it was indeed not mentioned.

### Other
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the inconsistency in the manuscript, sometimes referring to MCMC samples while actually meaning MCMC chains, and have revised the paper accordingly.

content.title: Addressing main concerns
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their insightful comments and for pointing out ways to improve our manuscript. In the following, we will elaborate on some more general remarks that have been noted across different comments.

### Bigger Picture and Predictive Performance
We would like to emphasize that the intent of our proposal is **not** to improve predictive performance. 
Rather, we argue for a more efficient use of MCMC by adjusting the number of chains to the functional diversity of the posterior, paving the way for more informed choices in the MCMC practice (Proposition 2).
In order to make posteriors interpretable and easier to approximate, we further suggest to remove symmetries post-hoc, the sole role of our proposed symmetry removal algorithm. In fact, we think that there is no other way to compute the true posterior without taking the induced symmetries into account. In short, we focus on inference rather than performance.
### Clarifications on Proposition 2 
Proposition 2 derives an upper bound for the number of chains as a practical guideline for the use of MCMC. Please note that this bound is not meant to be computed in exact fashion – as has been remarked, the number of unique posterior modes and their probability of occurrence are usually unknown quantities. It should instead be viewed as a means to gauge the number of chains resulting from reasonable assumptions based on domain knowledge or other research. Regarding the number of modes, we can safely disregard all equioutput-related ones, and evidence from recent work (e.g., high predictive performance of deep ensembles with very few members or of single-model-based Laplace approximations) as well as our own experiments (Section 6.3, Section 6.4) suggests that the remaining number of functionally diverse modes will be small. For mode probabilities, it might, for example, be interesting to compare the number of required chains for equally probable modes to a worst-case scenario with many highly unlikely ones.

### Network architecture size

We want to highlight that the proposed upper bound on MCMC chains given in Proposition 2 is independent from the neural network architecture (supported by Corollary 1) and can be applied to arbitrary neural networks exhibiting equioutput parametrizations. The challenging problem of removing permutation and activation related symmetries from the posterior distribution to uncover the reference set of unique parametrizations is a general problem that has yet to be solved completely. Therefore, aspects of future work will include scaling the approach to larger architectures. We would like to encourage readers to view this algorithm proposal as a proof-of-concept to enable superior posterior interpretability and approximation.

replying_to: Replying to Towards Efficient Posterior Sampling in Deep Neural Networks via Symmetry Removal
